content: Envy is an emotional state that arises when an individual perceives themselves as lacking a quality, achievement, or possession that another person has, and either desires to obtain it or wishes that the other person did not have it. This emotion can stem from feelings of low self-esteem, which are often triggered by upward social comparisons that threaten one’s self-image. When the envied individual is perceived as similar to the person experiencing envy, the intensity of the emotion is heightened, as it suggests that the envier could have been in the same position of possessing the desired object or quality. Bertrand Russell described envy as one of the most powerful causes of human unhappiness. It is a universal and deeply unfortunate aspect of human nature, as it not only leads the envious person to harbor ill will toward others but also causes personal dissatisfaction and unhappiness. Despite its negative connotations, Russell also argued that envy has played a role in driving societal progress, particularly in the pursuit of democracy, as it motivates individuals to strive for a more equitable social system. Envy and jealousy are distinct emotional experiences. Jealousy typically involves the fear of losing something one already possesses, often to another person, such as a loved one. In contrast, envy is characterized by the pain or frustration of seeing someone else possess something that one does not have. Envy generally involves two individuals, while jealousy often involves three. These emotions arise from different circumstances and should not be conflated. In philosophy, Aristotle defined envy as the pain caused by the good fortune of others. Immanuel Kant, on the other hand, described it as a reluctance to see one’s own well-being overshadowed by another’s, as people often measure their success not by its intrinsic value but by how it compares to the success of others. In the arts, envy is frequently associated with the color green, as reflected in phrases like green with envy or the green-eyed monster, a term popularized by Shakespeare in Othello. Shakespeare also referenced envy in The Merchant of Venice, where it is depicted as a powerful and consuming emotion capable of driving individuals to anger and aggression. Envy has been portrayed as a force that can dominate and control individuals, leading to destructive behaviors. For example, in romantic relationships, the discovery of a secret love can provoke intense envy, which may escalate into anger and even aggression. In religion, envy is considered one of the Seven Deadly Sins in Christian theology. The Book of Exodus explicitly warns against coveting a neighbor’s possessions, such as their house, spouse, or livestock, as this can lead to ungodly thoughts or actions. While it is natural to desire something that another person has, envy involves harboring negative feelings toward the person because of their possession. This distinction is critical, as envy is rooted in resentment and can lead to harmful consequences for both the envier and the envied.
